title: The Typewriter of Nagasaki's harbor
premise: In 1936, Paloma Blackwood, a half-foreign apprentice clockmaker in Nagasaki's harbor district, is hired to repair the observatory's master clock and discovers hidden inside it a Japanese naval officer's coded letters to his English lover. When their child is abandoned at her door with orders to forget the face, Paloma becomes the keeper of a secret that could hang them all. As war clouds gather, she must honor a peacetime promise to the now-declared enemy officer by smuggling the boy onto the last neutral ship before the morning tide — succeeding at the cost of her workshop, her anonymity, and nearly her life.
about_author: F. M. Okafor is the pen name of a former marine engineer who spent years in East Asian port cities collecting dockside stories from the last generation who remembered prewar Nagasaki. Okafor writes historical fiction about ordinary tradespeople caught in the machinery of empire.

chapters.title: The Clock That Ran Slow
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Summoned to the harbor observatory, she dismantles the master clock and finds oil-darkened letters sewn into its case. She pockets one, telling herself it's professional curiosity. The beat: quiet competence masking loneliness, and the first hook of a secret too heavy for one pair of hands.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At dawn, a wet nurse leaves a four-year-old boy, a bundle of yen, and instructions to forget her face. The child wears a locket matching the seal on the letters. Paloma realizes whose son he is. The beat: fear hardening into reluctant responsibility as she chooses not to turn him away.

chapters.title: Letters in Oil and Brass
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with flashback passages in the officer Ishikawa's voice through the letters. She decodes enough to learn of a peacetime promise: if ever war came, the child would go to his mother's people in England. The beat: intimacy with a stranger across time, and dread as she maps how far that promise will demand she go.

chapters.title: The Harbor Watch
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A Kempeitai sergeant begins visiting neighboring shops, asking about foreigners and missing children. Her mentor, old clockmaker Verhoeven, covers for her but warns that clocks are searched before ships sail. The beat: tightening surveillance; the safe world of gears gives way to a world of informers.

chapters.title: What Survival Costs
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She bribes a shipping clerk for passage papers and burns the most dangerous letter — then cannot bring herself to burn the rest. The boy calls her 'onee-chan' and she stops correcting him. The beat: the corrupting arithmetic of survival, where each compromise buys time and spends innocence.

chapters.title: The Sergeant's Offer
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The Kempeitai sergeant reveals he knows about the child and offers a trade: the letters' full contents in exchange for letting the boy 'disappear into an institution.' Paloma stalls, realizing he wants leverage over Ishikawa, not justice. The beat: open menace; power shows its face and asks her to become its instrument.

chapters.title: Verhoeven's Last Wind
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Verhoeven takes the blame for the missing papers and is detained; his shop is ransacked, her forged documents seized. He had known about the child all along. The beat: grief and fury — the price of survival paid by someone else — and Paloma's resolve turning from self-preservation to defiance.

chapters.title: Night Tide
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. With help from the wet nurse and a sympathetic stevedore, she moves the boy through the dockyards during a blackout drill, hiding inside the observatory's clock tower until the patrol passes. The beat: breathless suspense; every tick of the great clock above her counts down the hours to sailing.

chapters.title: The Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At the gangway, the sergeant confronts her — but Ishikawa, now disgraced and half-expecting arrest himself, arrives and claims the boy openly, shattering the sergeant's leverage. Paloma hands over the letters unburned. The beat: climax; truth offered freely defeats blackmail, and the promise is kept at last.

chapters.title: Setting the Hands Right
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, epilogue in 1946. Having survived the war and lost the observatory commission, she rebuilds a small shop by the harbor. A letter arrives from England: the boy, grown, remembers her face after all. She winds the repaired master clock one final time. The beat: bittersweet resolution — memory outlasting erasure, and survival redeemed by what was saved.
